desc:
Form as many disjoint pairs of elements of nums as possible, where a pair of two different positions i and j is allowed only if |nums[i] - nums[j]| ≥ d. Each position can be used in at most one pair, and you do not have to use all positions.

Return the maximum number of pairs.

nums = [1, 3, 5, 8, 10], d = 4   -> 2   (1 with 5, 3 with 8... or 1 with 8 and 3 with 10)
nums = [1, 3, 5, 8, 10], d = 8   -> 1   (only 1 with 10 has gap 9)
hints: Note that at most n // 2 pairs can exist at all. Sorting the array does not hurt: only values matter.
If k pairs are possible, then they can be chosen so that the k smallest numbers are matched with the k largest numbers. Why?
Binary search on k (feasibility is monotone): sort, then check that a[i] + d ≤ a[n - k + i] for every i < k, i.e. the i-th smallest is matched with the i-th of the k largest.
editorial: Sort the numbers. Suppose an optimal answer has k pairs. Exchange argument: using the k smallest values as the 'lower' members and the k largest values as the 'upper' members never hurts, since replacing a lower member with a smaller number or an upper member with a larger number can only increase gaps. Inside those two groups, pairing the i-th smallest with the i-th of the large group (in sorted order) is the best arrangement, because crossing pairs would shrink the smallest gap.
So k is feasible iff a[i + n - k] - a[i] ≥ d for all 0 ≤ i < k. If k works, k-1 works too, so binary search over k in [0, n//2]. Each check is O(k), total O(n log n) including the sort.
